title: Density Altitude — Why Hot, High, and Humid Aircraft Underperform

questions.text: An airport is at 6,000 feet MSL field elevation. The current altimeter setting is 29.52 in Hg. OAT is 25°C. Standard temperature at 6,000 feet is 3°C. What is the approximate density altitude?

options.label: A
options.text: 6,000 feet — field elevation equals pressure altitude when the altimeter setting is within 0.50 in Hg of standard; the temperature correction is already built into the altimeter reading and need not be applied separately

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately 8,640 feet — pressure altitude is approximately 6,400 feet (field elevation plus the altimeter setting correction: [29.92 − 29.52] × 1,000 = 400 feet); temperature deviation above standard is 25°C − 3°C = 22°C; DA penalty ≈ 22 × 120 = 2,640 feet; DA ≈ 6,400 + 2,640 = 9,040 feet

options.label: C
options.text: Approximately 9,040 feet — pressure altitude is approximately 6,400 feet; temperature deviation is 22°C above standard; DA penalty is 22 × 120 = 2,640 feet; density altitude ≈ 9,040 feet; the aircraft performs as if it were at over 9,000 feet despite being physically at 6,000 feet MSL

options.label: D
options.text: Approximately 7,200 feet — the standard density altitude formula adds 200 feet per degree Celsius above standard; at 22°C above standard the DA penalty is 4,400 feet; however, altimeter setting variations are excluded from the density altitude computation because pressure altitude is assumed equal to field elevation for DA purposes

questions.explanation: Density altitude calculation — two-step process: Step 1: Pressure Altitude. PA = field elevation + [(29.92 − altimeter setting) × 1,000]. PA = 6,000 + [(29.92 − 29.52) × 1,000] = 6,000 + 400 = 6,400 feet. Step 2: DA from temperature deviation. Standard temperature at 6,000 feet MSL: 15°C − (6 × 2°C) = 3°C. OAT = 25°C. Deviation = 25 − 3 = +22°C above standard. DA correction = 22 × 120 ≈ 2,640 feet. Density Altitude = 6,400 + 2,640 ≈ 9,040 feet. The aircraft's engine, propeller, and wings are all operating as if at 9,040 feet MSL — over 3,000 feet above the actual field elevation. Option A is wrong — the altimeter setting correction is NOT built into the altimeter setting-to-field elevation comparison; the 29.52 setting indicates below-standard pressure, raising PA above field elevation. Option B reaches the same DA but makes an arithmetic error in describing the process. Option D uses an incorrect 200 ft/°C multiplier (correct is ~120) and incorrectly excludes the altimeter setting correction.

questions.text: Which combination of conditions produces the HIGHEST density altitude and most severe aircraft performance degradation?

options.label: A
options.text: Sea level elevation, OAT 15°C, altimeter setting 29.92 in Hg, relative humidity 10% — standard sea-level conditions maximize air density and engine performance

options.label: B
options.text: 8,000 feet MSL, OAT 5°C (below standard), altimeter setting 30.50 in Hg, relative humidity 20% — cold temperature increases air density below standard, and higher-than-standard pressure compresses the air further, actually lowering density altitude below field elevation

options.label: C
options.text: 5,500 feet MSL, OAT 38°C, altimeter setting 29.42 in Hg, relative humidity 85% — high elevation, significantly above-standard temperature (standard at 5,500 ft = 4°C, deviation = +34°C), below-standard pressure, and extreme humidity all compound to maximize density altitude

options.label: D
options.text: 3,000 feet MSL, OAT 20°C, altimeter setting 29.82 in Hg, relative humidity 50% — moderate elevation with temperature 9°C above standard (standard at 3,000 ft = 9°C) produces the same DA as high-elevation airports because humidity doubles the temperature correction factor

questions.explanation: Density altitude is driven by three compounding factors: altitude, temperature above standard, and humidity. Option C combines all three at maximum adverse effect: (1) High elevation (5,500 feet) → baseline DA starts high. (2) OAT 38°C at 5,500 feet where standard temp is 4°C → deviation = +34°C → DA correction ≈ 34 × 120 = 4,080 feet. (3) Below-standard pressure (29.42 vs 29.92) → PA correction: (29.92 − 29.42) × 1,000 = +500 feet added to elevation. (4) Extreme humidity (85%) → approximately +200–300 feet additional DA equivalent not captured in standard formula. Total estimated DA: 5,500 + 500 (PA correction) + 4,080 (temp) + 250 (humidity estimate) ≈ 10,330 feet. The aircraft at 5,500 MSL on this day performs as if at over 10,000 feet. Option A describes exactly standard conditions — minimum density altitude. Option B has cold temperature (below standard) and high pressure — both reduce DA, creating better-than-standard performance. Option D makes a false claim that humidity doubles the temperature correction factor.

questions.text: A pilot uses the POH performance chart and enters the FIELD ELEVATION (4,800 feet) instead of the pressure altitude (5,200 feet) and OAT of 35°C instead of Celsius 35 (actual error: OAT was correctly in Celsius). The chart shows a takeoff distance of 1,850 feet. Available runway is 2,200 feet. The actual takeoff distance at correct inputs would require approximately 2,300 feet. What is the consequence?

options.label: A
options.text: No consequence — the 350-foot error in PA entry (4,800 vs. 5,200 feet) is within the POH chart's built-in safety margin of 500 feet; POH takeoff distances include a 15% safety buffer that absorbs minor input errors

options.label: B
options.text: The pilot will likely overrun the runway — the field elevation input (4,800 feet) underestimates the density altitude, producing a calculated distance (1,850 feet) significantly shorter than the actual required distance (approximately 2,300 feet); the available runway (2,200 feet) is insufficient for the true takeoff distance, but the pilot believes a 350-foot margin exists when in fact a 100-foot deficit exists

options.label: C
options.text: The pilot is safe — the 2,200-foot available runway exceeds the charted 1,850-foot required distance by 350 feet; even if the true distance is 2,300 feet, the 15% FAA-required POH safety factor added to all POH charts reduces the effective required distance to 1,995 feet which is within the 2,200-foot runway

options.label: D
options.text: The consequence is regulatory only — 14 CFR 91.103 requires a performance calculation before every flight; using field elevation instead of pressure altitude violates 91.103 but does not substantively affect actual aircraft performance because takeoff rolls vary by less than 5% between field elevation and pressure altitude

questions.explanation: This scenario illustrates the real-world consequence of incorrect POH chart inputs. The pilot calculated 1,850 feet required (using understated DA from field elevation entry), believed a comfortable 350-foot margin existed, and committed to a takeoff on a 2,200-foot runway. The actual required distance at correct DA inputs is 2,300 feet — 100 feet more than available runway. The pilot will almost certainly overrun. This is the exact mechanism behind multiple fatal density altitude accidents documented by NTSB. Option A invents a 500-foot built-in safety buffer that does not exist — POH distances are calculated to STANDARD speeds and obstacle clearance is not a built-in 'margin.' Option C invents an FAA-required 15% safety factor added to POH charts — POH distances for takeoff roll are actual calculated distances, not pre-inflated with a safety buffer. Option D minimizes the DA error as a regulatory technicality — a 400-foot pressure altitude difference combined with high temperature creates 20-30% difference in takeoff roll, not 5%.

questions.text: A pilot is conducting a VFR cross-country in January over mountainous terrain in Colorado. OAT at cruise altitude is -25°C. Standard temperature at cruise altitude is -9°C. The altimeter reads 10,500 feet with current altimeter setting dialed in. What is the likely relationship between indicated altitude and true altitude?

options.label: A
options.text: True altitude equals indicated altitude — the altimeter setting accounts for all temperature variations; the Kollsman window adjustment fully corrects for non-standard temperature so that the indicated altitude equals the actual altitude above sea level at all times

options.label: B
options.text: True altitude is HIGHER than indicated altitude — in cold air that is less dense than standard, the pressure gradient compresses over a shorter vertical distance; the altimeter reading anticipates standard air density and overestimates actual altitude; the aircraft is actually higher than 10,500 feet

options.label: C
options.text: True altitude is LOWER than indicated — in cold air, which is denser than standard, the pressure gradient exists over a shorter vertical distance than assumed by the altimeter; the altimeter reads high, meaning the aircraft is actually below the indicated altitude of 10,500 feet; the mnemonic is 'from high to low (temperature), look out below'

options.label: D
options.text: True altitude is lower than indicated, but only by approximately 50 feet per 10°C below standard; at 16°C below standard (-25°C vs -9°C standard), the error is approximately 80 feet — negligible for VFR terrain clearance purposes at 10,500 feet MSL

options.label: E
options.text: True altitude cannot be determined from temperature and altimeter reading alone — true altitude requires GPS confirmation and the altimeter indication at that altitude is meaningless without RAIM verification

questions.explanation: This question tests the cold-temperature altimetry error — one of the most consequential physics effects in mountain flying. When outside air temperature is well below standard (ISA), the air is denser than the altimeter assumes. This means the pressure decreases more quickly with altitude than the standard model predicts. The altimeter assumes the ISA pressure gradient; in cold dense air, the same pressure reading corresponds to a LOWER actual altitude. The altimeter reads HIGH — the aircraft is lower than indicated. Mnemonic: 'From HIGH to low (temperature), look out BELOW' — the aircraft is below the altimeter reading. At -25°C (16°C below standard), the altitude error at 10,500 feet can be 300-600 feet — meaningful in mountainous terrain at night or in IMC. CFIT (Controlled Flight Into Terrain) accidents have occurred when pilots assumed indicated altitude equaled terrain clearance in severe cold. Option B describes the opposite error. Option D significantly underestimates the correction magnitude — the FAA cold temperature correction table in AIM 7-2-3 shows corrections well above 50 feet per 10°C at altitude.

questions.text: On a warm, humid day (OAT 95°F, relative humidity 90%), a pilot attempts a single-engine piston takeoff from a sea-level airport on a standard altimeter setting. Density altitude is calculated as approximately 3,800 feet. The pilot expects a normal takeoff because 'the airport is at sea level.' What is the expected performance impact?

options.label: A
options.text: No impact — density altitude calculations apply only to high-elevation airports; sea-level airports are definitionally at standard atmospheric pressure and the DA formula produces a result that is always within 200 feet of field elevation at sea-level airports

options.label: B
options.text: Significant degraded performance — at a DA of 3,800 feet, the engine produces approximately 10-15% less power than at sea level; the propeller generates less thrust; and the wings require a higher groundspeed (TAS) to produce the same lift; takeoff roll will be substantially longer than the POH sea-level chart value, and initial climb rate will be reduced

options.label: C
options.text: Minor impact only — engine performance is affected by altitude but not temperature or humidity; at sea level, the intake manifold pressure guarantees full sea-level power regardless of OAT or humidity; only aircraft above 8,000 feet DA experience meaningful engine power reduction

options.label: D
options.text: The pilot is correct to expect normal performance — the POH sea-level charts include atmospheric correction tables for up to 100°F temperatures; consulting the 'hot day' column in the POH eliminates the density altitude concern automatically for sea-level and near-sea-level airports

questions.explanation: At a density altitude of 3,800 feet, the aircraft is operating as if physically at 3,800 feet MSL — despite being at sea level. The performance impacts are real and significant regardless of field elevation: (1) Engine: non-turbocharged engines lose approximately 3% power per 1,000 feet of density altitude. At 3,800 DA, power loss ≈ 11-14%. (2) Propeller: operates in less dense air, generating proportionally less thrust for the same RPM. (3) Wings: require higher TAS to generate the same lift — takeoff roll increases because the aircraft must accelerate to a higher ground/indicated airspeed to generate liftoff velocity in thin air... actually, in this case the IAS liftoff speed stays the same but the TAS is higher, so with the same IAS, the aircraft is moving faster over the ground — increasing the runway distance required. NTSB data shows numerous GA overruns at sea-level airports on hot humid days when pilots assumed sea-level performance from POH sea-level charts. Option A invents a 'sea-level airports are always standard' claim. Option C falsely claims only altitude matters, not temperature/humidity. Option D invents universal 'hot day' POH tables that compensate for DA concerns.

questions.text: Under 14 CFR 91.103, is a private pilot legally required to compute takeoff performance data including density altitude before each flight?

options.label: A
options.text: No — 14 CFR 91.103 requires familiarity with weather reports, NOTAMs, and fuel requirements, but does not specifically mandate takeoff performance calculations; performance computation is a best practice recommended in the AIM but is not a legal requirement under Part 91

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — 14 CFR 91.103(b) requires the pilot in command to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, specifically including 'for a flight not under IFR' the runway lengths at airports of intended use, and the aircraft's performance information; this encompasses takeoff distance computation at current DA conditions

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — but only for Part 91 flights conducted with passengers on board; solo pilot training flights under 14 CFR 61.51 are exempt from the performance computation requirement because CFI supervision provides an independent performance check

options.label: D
options.text: No — performance computation requirements for private pilots are established in the PTS (Practical Test Standard) and apply only during the checkride evaluation; post-checkride Part 91 flights are governed by pilot judgment, not a performance calculation mandate

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.103 establishes a clear preflight information requirement for PICs. For VFR flights specifically, 91.103(b) requires the PIC to become familiar with 'runway lengths at airports of intended use' and 'takeoff and landing distance data' from the AFM (Aircraft Flight Manual) or Pilot's Operating Handbook. Performance computation that accounts for current density altitude is not optional — it is legally mandated for every Part 91 flight. Flying with only a vague sense of 'it'll be fine' without computing actual takeoff distances at current DA is a regulatory violation in addition to a safety failure. Option A incorrectly limits 91.103 to weather and NOTAMs — the regulation explicitly lists runway length and performance data. Option C invents a solo-flight exemption from performance requirements — 91.103 applies to PIC regardless of whether passengers are aboard. Option D misidentifies the ACS as the source of the performance requirement and incorrectly limits it to checkrides.

questions.text: On a July afternoon in Telluride, Colorado (TEX, elevation 9,070 feet MSL), a pilot plans to depart with two passengers and full fuel. OAT is 85°F, altimeter setting 29.72. The pilot computes DA at approximately 12,800 feet. The POH shows service ceiling of 14,000 feet and maximum rate of climb at DA 12,000 feet is 200 FPM. The pilot thinks: 'We have 1,200 feet to the service ceiling — I can still climb out.' What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.label: A
options.text: The reasoning is correct — 200 FPM climb rate exceeds the FAA minimum required altitude gain of 100 FPM for departure; at full gross weight with three occupants and full fuel, 200 FPM is sufficient to clear terrain and reach cruise altitude safely

options.label: B
options.text: Critical errors: (1) DA is 12,800 feet — nearly at the service ceiling; 'service ceiling' is defined as where climb rate is 100 FPM at MAXIMUM GROSS WEIGHT under standard conditions; with full fuel, passengers, and above-standard temperature, actual climb rate at 12,800 DA will be far less than the charted 200 FPM at 12,000 DA; (2) Surrounding terrain in Telluride exceeds 14,000 feet MSL; departing with marginal climb performance from within a valley surrounded by 14,000-foot peaks with 200 FPM or less available is potentially unsurvivable if engine performance is below chart values

options.label: C
options.text: The reasoning is flawed only because full fuel and three passengers exceed the max gross weight for this airport; if the pilot reduces fuel load to below half tanks, DA performance will remain the same but the aircraft will climb at the full 200 FPM as charted

options.label: D
options.text: The reasoning is acceptable — Telluride departures with 200 FPM climb rate are common in summer; local pilots accept marginal performance margins as part of mountain flying; the 14,000-foot service ceiling provides adequate buffer for a standard Telluride departure on any runway direction

questions.explanation: This is the classic mountain density altitude trap that has killed pilots repeatedly. The multi-layered errors: (1) Service ceiling is defined at STANDARD conditions at gross weight — 100 FPM remaining climb rate. At 12,800 DA (800 feet above the charted 12,000 DA performance point), the 200 FPM chart value is already borderline. Real-world performance with non-standard temperature, passengers, and humidity will reduce actual climb rate further — possibly to 50-80 FPM. (2) Telluride is surrounded by the San Juan Mountains, with peaks exceeding 14,000 feet MSL in every departure direction. A pilot departing with 100-200 FPM climb rate in a box canyon with no go-around terrain has essentially zero margin for any performance shortfall. (3) The 'we have headroom to service ceiling' reasoning ignores that service ceiling is a FLOOR, not a safety margin. Options C and D represent classic Macho-Get-There-Itis: rationalizing marginal performance as acceptable because 'local pilots do it' or because reducing fuel magically restores climb rate without addressing the core DA issue.
questions.sjt_rationale: Get-There-Itis and Macho drive the willingness to depart from Telluride in these conditions. The correct action: delay until cooler morning temperatures (DA drops significantly), reduce payload, or choose an alternate route/airport. Multiple NTSB accident reports document identical scenarios at Telluride and similar high-DA Rocky Mountain airports.

questions.text: Before departure, a pilot consults the POH takeoff chart using field elevation (3,500 feet) and gets a computed takeoff roll of 1,600 feet. Available runway is 2,000 feet — appears comfortable. The pilot did not compute pressure altitude or density altitude. The actual pressure altitude is 3,900 feet, OAT is 30°C above standard, yielding a true DA of approximately 8,600 feet. At DA 8,600, the POH shows takeoff roll of 2,700 feet. What is the SAFEST action?

options.label: A
options.text: Depart — the 400-foot difference in computed vs. actual takeoff distances is within the acceptable deviation for visual conditions under 14 CFR 91.103; the 2,000-foot runway exceeds the original 1,600-foot computed distance and the pilot-in-command has authority to determine acceptable risk margins

options.label: B
options.text: DO NOT DEPART — the correct performance calculation shows 2,700 feet required vs. 2,000 feet available; this is a 700-foot runway deficit; the pilot should identify options: wait for cooler conditions (early morning temperatures), reduce payload to reduce gross weight, use a longer runway if available at the airport, or divert to an airport with a longer runway

options.label: C
options.text: Depart and accelerate to rotation speed as fast as possible — applying maximum power from the very beginning of the takeoff roll reduces the DA penalty; full power acceleration compensates for the density altitude error and will result in a takeoff within the 2,000 feet available

options.label: D
options.text: Add 10% to the computed distance as the standard safety margin per AIM advisory — 1,600 feet × 1.10 = 1,760 feet; since 1,760 is still below 2,000 available, the departure is acceptable; POH distances are always calculated conservatively so real performance will always be better than charted

questions.explanation: The correct performance calculation (DA 8,600 feet) shows 2,700 feet REQUIRED vs. 2,000 feet AVAILABLE. This is a 700-foot deficit. The departure as planned would likely result in a runway overrun — potentially at rotation speed, with no remaining paved surface. The correct action is to NOT DEPART under current conditions and identify remedies: (a) WAIT: DA drops significantly with cooler temperatures — early morning can reduce DA by 1,000-2,000 feet at the same airport. (b) REDUCE PAYLOAD: remove passengers or cargo to reduce gross weight, which reduces required takeoff distance. (c) USE LONGER RUNWAY: many airports have multiple runways of different lengths. (d) DIVERT: fly to an airport with a sufficiently long runway for current DA conditions. Option A is Invulnerability — rationalizing a 700-foot runway deficit as within 'acceptable deviation.' Option C is Macho — there is no technique that overcomes a 700-foot runway deficit from incorrect DA. Option D invents a universal 10% AIM advisory margin that does not exist and would not solve a 700-foot deficit regardless.
questions.sjt_rationale: The core failure is Complacency in the preflight performance check — field elevation instead of pressure altitude produces a false sense of adequate runway. The safety reckoning moment is when the correct calculation is made. The correct ADM is: data shows the departure is not safe, therefore the departure does not happen.
